source_text: For a clearer view of binding, switch to a smaller example. In the Experiment menu it is called Live nucleosome access, twenty-five point six kilobases. That simply means a twenty-five point six kilobase stretch of chromatin: one hundred twenty-eight beads, still two hundred base pairs each, set up so that nucleosomes visibly control which sites proteins can reach. Open the one-dimensional genome and choose Live binding. Genes, nucleosome occupancy and directly bound proteins share one genomic axis. Navigate to a gene, then use Binding detail to see individual sites. Each molecule marker comes from a real chromatin bond; proximity alone is not binding. Run to watch bindings change, then pause and select a site. The table gives two rates for each protein. The association hazard is how often a nearby molecule binds, per unit of time. The release hazard is how often a bound molecule lets go; one over the release hazard is the average time it stays bound. Times remain reduced until an empirical physical mapping is attached. All tracks restores the wider view of marks, loops, polymerases and protein preferences.
